question: Concerns have been raised about the plight of foreign workers in the Netherlands1. Many are citizens of other EU Member States employed by temporary employment agencies. One cause of concern is the ‘agency clause’: a contractual arrangement between the temporary employment agency and the employee that means the employee’s posting to a user company can be ended at any time.

In practice, this makes it possible for people to be sacked on the spot. There are also restrictions on the registration of these workers, for whom the temporary employment agencies often arrange accommodation in camps or hostels. Many local authorities only allow these people to sign up to a register for non-residents, which is designed for short stays or exceptional situations.
This makes it difficult for them to pay state pension contributions and reduces medical coverage. In view of this: 1.
Does the Commission take the view that the regulation of workers employed by temporary employment agencies might result in indirect discrimination in the Netherlands?
Does the Commission consider the restrictions on the ordinary registration of EU workers in the Netherlands to be consistent with the principle of free movement?
What steps is the Commission intending to take to address these problems for intra-EU workers in the Netherlands?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.3.2024) The so-called agency clauses which regulate the duration of the contract between the temporary work agency and the employee, are matters within the remit of the national legislator and/or enforcement authorities.

In 2023, crucial legislation and regulations entered into force or were initiated1 by the Dutch government to structurally improve the position of EU-mobile workers in the Netherlands, such as a bill aiming at the protection of workers in the temporary employment sector and the exclusion of rogue parties from the market; the amendment of the Basic Registration of Persons Act (BRP) for a better overview of the residence situation of mobile EU citizens and an Act around ‘Good Landlordship’ aimed at tackling housing abuses.

Concerning the registration of EU workers, Directive 2004/38/EC2 foresees that for stays up to three months (Article 5(5)) Member States may only require to report presence within a reasonable and non-discriminatory period. For residence beyond three months, a Member State may require an EU citizen to register with the relevant authorities (Article 8(1)).

Residence registration under the said Directive must be distinguished from registration in a national or local population register like the BRP, which is a matter for national law alone. Neither form of registration is a condition for lawful residence under EU law.

For what concerns the posting of workers, including by a temporary employment agency, under Directive 96/71/EC3, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/9574, the Commission is reviewing the application and implementation of the latter Directive, as foreseen in its Article 2. The Commission intends to submit the report to the European Parliament in the first half of 2024.
